metric.capability_coverage.formula: C = 100 * (sum over 44 probes of capability_points(2) * support_factor) / 88
metric.capability_coverage.methodology_note: Capability Coverage is computed on the full fixed 88-point denominator (all 44 probes), independent of the common-basis rule used for metrics A-D. Support level (FULL/PARTIAL/NONE) is assigned per the frozen rubric's deterministic tie-break question; PARTIAL always carries the applicable P-letter(s), NONE always carries the N-reason and citation.
metric.capability_coverage.na_policy_compliance: No probe was removed, reweighted, or marked N/A because Python lacks a capability (NA-1, NA-3, NA-6). Every NONE/PARTIAL above carries a written rule citation (NA-5). NONE totals: F04.P1, F04.P2, F05.P2, F20.P2 (4 of 44 probes, 9.1%), well under the V4 one-third-of-probes suspicious-column threshold.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §4.2 Naming and binding (all names are rebindable via assignment; no `const`/`let`/final-local form exists).
per_probe.rationale: Python has no non-reassignable local binding form; the only mechanism is plain assignment `n = 7`, which can always be rebound. Substituted weaker mechanism.

per_probe.citation: PEP 8 'Constants' section (convention only, no enforcement); Python Language Reference §4.2.
per_probe.rationale: Python has no compile-time/immutable constant declaration form; `LIMIT = 100` at module scope is an ordinary rebindable name, distinguished from `counter` only by naming convention (PEP 8 UPPER_CASE), not by language-enforced immutability.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §4.2 Naming and binding; §7.2 (assignment statements) — no separate declaration syntax.
per_probe.rationale: Python has no declaration-without-initializer statement; there is no way to declare `v` before the branch. The branch/read pattern is expressible by omitting a prior declaration and assigning `v` in both arms, which delivers the observable behavior but substitutes a weaker mechanism (no explicit 'uninitialized declaration' construct; unassigned names raise UnboundLocalError dynamically rather than being statically declared).

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `bytearray`/`bytes` constructors: 'an object of the given length, initialized with null bytes'.
per_probe.rationale: Named substitution per R9: Python's `bytearray(16)` (or `bytes(16)`) is always zero-initialized; there is no documented way to obtain genuinely uninitialized bulk storage. Substituted with the default-initialized 16-element buffer as directed by the canonical_task's own substitution clause.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.2.1 (Augmented assignment statements).
per_probe.rationale: `x += 1` is the standard in-place update form for a mutable local scalar name in Python; the name binding is updated so a subsequent read of `x` observes the increment.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.3.1 (Assignment to subscript).
per_probe.rationale: `xs[1] = 42` mutates the list object in place through the existing name; standard, minimal, idiomatic.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §4.2; Data Model §3.1 (int objects are immutable) — no documented alias-to-scalar mechanism exists.
per_probe.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
per_probe.rationale: Python ints are immutable and there is no reference/pointer/inout mechanism giving two names write access to the same scalar storage in the same scope; no fragment is written per R9/N-4.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs — no read-only sequence view type documented for `list`; `types.MappingProxyType` exists only for mappings.
per_probe.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
per_probe.rationale: Python has no non-copying, read-only (write-protected) view type over a plain list. A second name bound to the same list (`window = xs`) is a non-copying alias but is fully writable, not read-only; there is no standard immutable/read-only view construct for `list` (unlike `types.MappingProxyType` for dict, no list analogue exists).

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.10.3 (Identity comparisons, `is`); Data Model §3.1 (every object has an identity, `id()`).
per_probe.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
per_probe.rationale: Python objects have identity distinct from value equality; `is` performs reference-identity comparison. Routing `first` through a one-element list and reading it back as `second` obtains a second handle to the same object, and `first is second` is True.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §7.3.4 (Call expressions); §4.2 (argument passing passes object references, 'call by object').
per_probe.rationale: Ordinary call syntax `f(x)` is Python's plain call form; it passes the object reference and is the required REQUIRED spec-6.1.4.B probe form.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §4.2, §7.6 (function definitions) — parameters are local names bound to the passed object; no writable-alias parameter form exists for immutable scalars.
per_probe.rationale: Python has no documented way for a callee to write a caller's scalar (int) local variable — ints are immutable and there is no `&`/`ref`/`inout`/pointer form. Wrapping the integer in a mutable container is explicitly excluded as a FULL substitute by the canonical_task, and no other standard mechanism exists.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §7.6 (function definitions, closures); §6.2.9 (lambda); stdlib `map()` builtin.
per_probe.rationale: Python closures (nested `def` or `lambda`) capture enclosing-scope names by reference to the object at call time; `neg` capturing `k` and passed by name to `map(neg, xs)` is fully standard.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §8.6 (return statement).
per_probe.rationale: `mid(xs)` returning `xs[1]`, bound to `y`, then returned, is fully ordinary Python.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.2.3 (Assignment statements, target lists / tuple unpacking); §6.12 (expression lists forming tuples).
per_probe.rationale: Python's standard multi-result mechanism is tuple return with unpacking: `return a//b, a%b` and `q, r = divmod2(a,b)`.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.17 (Operator precedence).
per_probe.rationale: `r = a * b + c` uses ordinary operator precedence (`*` binds tighter than `+`).

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.7 (Binary arithmetic operations) — `//` floor division, `%` modulo, `/` true division always float.
per_probe.rationale: `q = a // b` (floor division), `m = a % b` (remainder, sign follows divisor per Python semantics), `d = a / b` requires no explicit conversion since `/` always yields float in Python 3.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §3.2 (int has 'unlimited precision'); no `int32`/checked/wrapping/saturating arithmetic exists in the core language.
per_probe.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
per_probe.rationale: Python has no fixed-width (32-bit) integer type or named maximum for one; `int` is arbitrary-precision and never overflows. The fragment can only simulate a nominal 32-bit maximum with a literal (2**31-1) and compute `m+1`, which simply widens without any of the checked/wrapping/saturating rungs the probe asks about — a substituted weaker mechanism, since the language provides no fixed-width integer capability at all.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.7 — `//` raises ZeroDivisionError on zero divisor; explicit guard is the standard idiom.
per_probe.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
per_probe.rationale: Rung (ii) explicit guard on `b == 0` selecting a fallback of 0 is available and used since Python has no rung-(i) checked-division-to-optional standard operation; using the next available rung, as the canonical_task itself permits, is FULL, not PARTIAL, because determinacy of rung choice is not a support criterion.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.10.2 (Value comparisons) — `str.__eq__` compares character sequences.
per_probe.rationale: `s1 == s2` for `str` compares character contents (value equality), never identity, by documented language semantics.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `list.sort(*, key=None, reverse=False)`.
per_probe.rationale: `xs.sort(reverse=True)` sorts the list in place using the explicit `reverse=True` argument (non-default order supplied explicitly); `a < b` is the ordinary less-than operator.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `ctypes` module — fixed-width simple C data types truncate/wrap per C semantics on assignment.
per_probe.rationale: `ctypes.c_int32(big).value` is Python's standard-library (ctypes, no third-party package) documented 32-bit truncating/wrapping conversion, used here as the FULL-satisfying rung.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.7 (Binary arithmetic operations) — mixed int/float arithmetic converts the int operand to float.
per_probe.rationale: `sum = i + d` implicitly promotes the `int` operand to `float`; no explicit conversion syntax is required or written, matching the language's normal implicit-conversion rule.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.3.1 (Subscriptions) — raises `IndexError` when index out of range.
per_probe.rationale: `e = xs[i]` is the ordinary indexed-read form; out-of-range raises `IndexError`, a documented, deterministic outcome recoverable from the fragment.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §6.3.1 (Slicings) — slicing a list returns a new list object.
per_probe.rationale: `part = xs[1:4]` is Python's standard slicing form; list slicing is documented to always produce a new list (a copy), which is itself the determinate, documented answer for metric B/D purposes.

per_probe.citation: PEP 604 (`X | None` union syntax); Python Language Reference §6.12 (conditional expressions).
per_probe.rationale: `o: int | None = None` expresses the type-level optional via PEP 604/typing union syntax with the explicit absent sentinel `None`; `n = o if o is not None else 0` is used as the fallback form since Python provides no dedicated coalescing operator (canonical_task permits hand-written form only when the language provides no dedicated form, which is the case here).

per_probe.citation: No such construct documented in Python Language Reference or stdlib `typing`/`operator` modules.
per_probe.rationale: Named substitution per R9: Python has no standard optional-aware chaining/mapping/safe-call operation (no `Maybe.map`, no `?.`). The explicit conditional form is written instead, as directed.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `int(x)` — raises `ValueError` if `x` is not a valid literal; Language Reference §8 (uncaught exceptions propagate to caller).
per_probe.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
per_probe.rationale: `int(s)` raises `ValueError` on malformed input; leaving it uncaught inside `parse_twice` propagates the exception to the caller automatically — Python's normal, idiomatic propagation mechanism.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §8.4 (The try statement).
per_probe.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
per_probe.rationale: `try: n = int(s) except ValueError: n = 0` is the ordinary local-handling construct.

per_probe.citation: PEP 591 (`typing.final`) — 'type checkers should prohibit'; not enforced by the interpreter. Python Data Model — classes are open to subclassing anywhere by default.
per_probe.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
per_probe.rationale: Named substitution per R9: Python has no language-enforced closed/sealed alternative set. `typing.final`/`@final` is a static-analysis-only hint (mypy), not enforced by the CPython runtime; nothing in the language itself prevents a third subclass elsewhere. Substituted with the nearest standard construct: an ordinary (open) class hierarchy for `Shape`/`Circle`/`Rect`.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §8.7.2 (`match` statement) — no exhaustiveness checking is performed by the interpreter; a non-matching subject with no wildcard case simply executes no branch.
per_probe.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
per_probe.rationale: Python's `match` statement (3.10+) provides case dispatch, but does not statically or dynamically guarantee exhaustiveness over a class hierarchy — an unmatched value with no wildcard `_` simply falls through with no error, so the exhaustiveness guarantee the canonical_task asks about is undocumented/unspecified rather than enforced.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §5 (The import system); Data Model — classes/subclasses may be defined in any module.
per_probe.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
per_probe.rationale: Python's module system and open class hierarchy trivially allow a new `Tri` class implementing `area()` to be defined in a separate module and dispatched through the abstract interface (duck typing / ABC), without modifying `shapes.py`.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §4 (data model, duck typing); no declaration-site generic syntax required for reuse across types.
per_probe.rationale: `def head(xs): return xs[0]` is generic over element type by duck typing without any special generic syntax, reusable at `list[int]` and `list[str]` call sites.

per_probe.citation: PEP 695 (type parameter syntax) and PEP 484 (`TypeVar`) — both documented as static-typing constructs; CPython does not enforce bounds at runtime.
per_probe.rationale: Named substitution per R9: Python 3.12 type-parameter syntax (`def max_of[T: SupportsRichComparison](a: T, b: T) -> T`) or a `TypeVar(bound=...)` can state a constraint, but it is checked only by external static type checkers (mypy/pyright), not enforced by the CPython runtime at declaration or call time — misuse is diagnosed nowhere at runtime.

per_probe.citation: Python Data Model §3.3 (attribute lookup / method resolution is dynamic, per-instance).
per_probe.rationale: A plain Python list can hold instances of `A` and `B` (both exposing `.tag()`); `items[0].tag()` dispatches at runtime via normal attribute lookup, with no static element type recoverable, i.e. genuine heterogeneous runtime dispatch through duck typing.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, builtin `sum(iterable, /, start=0)`.
per_probe.rationale: `xs = [1, 2, 3]; total = sum(xs)` uses the standard builtin `sum()` reduction.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `dict.values()`, `dict.get(key, default)`.
per_probe.rationale: `mp = {"a": 1}; total = sum(mp.values()); miss = mp.get("b", 0)` uses standard dict iteration and default-supplying lookup.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §8.5 (The with statement); stdlib `io` docs — file objects are context managers whose `__exit__` closes the file.
per_probe.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
per_probe.rationale: `with open("data.txt") as f: text = f.read()` guarantees the file is closed at the end of the `with` block on every exit path, including when `read()` raises.

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §3.1/§3.4 (`object.__del__`) — 'It is not guaranteed that `__del__` methods are called for objects that still exist when the interpreter exits'; CPython implementation notes state refcounting-based promptness is a CPython-specific detail, not a language guarantee.
per_probe.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
per_probe.rationale: Named substitution per R9: `__del__` is Python's end-of-lifetime hook, but the language reference explicitly leaves the exact timing of finalization as an implementation detail (CPython's refcounting makes it near-deterministic for acyclic objects; other implementations such as PyPy/Jython do not guarantee this), so the deterministic, exactly-once guarantee the canonical_task asks for is not a normative language guarantee.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, builtin function `print()` — always available without import.
per_probe.rationale: `print("x")` uses the builtin `print` function; no import is required, which the canonical_task explicitly allows ('or nothing if the facility is available without one').

per_probe.citation: Python Language Reference §5 (The import system) / PEP 8 — leading underscore is 'a weak internal use indicator' with no runtime enforcement (aside from `from module import *`, which module-level `_name`s are merely excluded from, not blocked from direct reference).
per_probe.rationale: Python module-level privacy is convention-only: a leading underscore (`_secret`) signals non-public but is not enforced by the interpreter — `util._secret()` remains callable from outside `util`. The canonical_task itself directs PARTIAL under P-a when the private boundary cannot be enforced.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `concurrent.futures` module; `asyncio` module.
per_probe.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
per_probe.rationale: `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` (or `asyncio.gather`) launches two concurrent units, joins both, and combines results — a standard-library concurrency facility shipped with the frozen toolchain.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `threading.Lock` — 'This class implements primitive lock objects... used to synchronize access.'
per_probe.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
per_probe.rationale: `threading.Lock` explicitly guards each increment of the shared counter from two threads; this is an explicit, standard-library synchronization construct (not reliance on the GIL alone), documented to make the guarded critical section race-free, verified by repeated runs.

per_probe.citation: Python stdlib docs, `ctypes` module — 'ctypes is a foreign function library for Python. It provides C compatible data types, and allows calling functions in DLLs or shared libraries.'
per_probe.rationale: `ctypes.CDLL(None).abs(-3)` (or platform libc load) calls the C standard library `abs` function using Python's built-in `ctypes` FFI mechanism, shipped with the frozen toolchain, no third-party package.

per_probe.citation: Rubric text: 'For a language that produces NO compiled artifact under its frozen recipe, the N-reason is N-1 and the nm field of the evidence record reads "no compiled artifact under the frozen recipe".'
per_probe.nm_field: no compiled artifact under the frozen recipe
per_probe.rationale: Python's frozen recipe (`python3 FILE.py`) produces no compiled artifact at all; there is no mechanism in the language to export a stable, unmangled, C-ABI symbol from a `.py` file for an external `nm` check. Per the rubric's own guidance, this is recorded as NONE (N-1) with the artifact note, not as N/A.
